{{Short description|American chemist (1929–2022)}}
'''Edward Malcolm Kosower''' (February 2, 1929 – April 7, 2022) was{{Citation needed|date=September 2023|reason=Death needs a source}} an American-Israeli chemist.

Kosower was born in Brooklyn, New York on February 2, 1929 and attended high school at [[Stuyvesant High School|Stuyvesant]], where he was a classmate of fellow chemist [[Andrew Streitwieser]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://cen.acs.org/articles/87/i9/Roger-Adams-Award-Organic-Chemistry.html|title=Roger Adams Award In Organic Chemistry {{!}} March 2, 2009 Issue - Vol. 87 Issue 9 {{!}} Chemical & Engineering News|last=Tullo|first=Alexander H.|website=cen.acs.org|access-date=2018-08-18}}</ref>

He received his B.S. degree from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 1948 and Ph.D. from the University of California, Los Angeles in 1952 under the mentorship of [[Saul Winstein]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://academictree.org/chemistry/tree.php?pid=55525|title=Chemistry Tree - Edward M. Kosower Family Tree|website=academictree.org|access-date=2018-08-15}}</ref>  After postdoctoral research at Basel with [[Cyril Grob]], and then at Harvard with [[Frank Westheimer]], he began his independent career as assistant professor at Lehigh University (1954) and the University of Wisconsin (1956).  In 1961, he moved to Stony Brook University as associate professor where he was later promoted to full professor.  In 1972, he moved to Tel Aviv University, where he was named the Josef Kryss Professor of Biophysical Organic Chemistry in 1992.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://en-exact-sciences.tau.ac.il/profile/kosower|title=Prof. Edward Kosower {{!}} Faculty of Exact Sciences Raymond & Beverly Sackler|website=en-exact-sciences.tau.ac.il|language=en-US|access-date=2018-08-15}}</ref>

He was a Guggenheim Fellow from 1977 to 1978, and was a member of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]].

He is best known for his earlier work in [[physical organic chemistry]] and later work in biophysical chemistry.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Kosower|first=Edward|date=1997|title=Rethinking Physical Organic Chemistry|url=https://www.iupac.org/publications/pac/1997/pdf/6902x0249.pdf|journal=Pure Appl. Chem.|volume=69|issue=2|pages=249–257|doi=10.1351/pac199769020249|s2cid=97625509}}</ref>  In particular, he developed the ''Z'' scale for [[Chemical polarity|solvent polarity]] based on the [[solvatochromic]] effect for [[zwitterionic]] dyes and investigated [[bimane]] dyes as fluorescent labels.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Kosower|first=Edward M.|date=July 1958|title=The Effect of Solvent on Spectra. I. A New Empirical Measure of Solvent Polarity: Z-Values|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|language=en|volume=80|issue=13|pages=3253–3260|doi=10.1021/ja01546a020|bibcode=1958JAChS..80.3253K |issn=0002-7863}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kosower|first1=Nechama S.|last2=Kosower|first2=Edward M.|last3=Newton|first3=Gerald L.|last4=Ranney|first4=Helen M.|date=1979|title=Bimane Fluorescent Labels: Labeling of Normal Human Red Cells under Physiological Conditions|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|volume=76|issue=7|pages=3382–3386|jstor=69995|doi=10.1073/pnas.76.7.3382|pmid=291011|pmc=383829|bibcode=1979PNAS...76.3382K|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Kosower is the author of an early textbook on physical organic chemistry, ''An Introduction to Physical Organic Chemistry'' (Wiley, 1968), and joined Streitwieser and [[Clayton Heathcock|Heathcock]] as coauthor of the 4th edition of their influential textbook, ''Introduction to Organic Chemistry'' (Macmillan, 1992).
